title: What Master Vasht Wrote

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Nineteenth Saying: Confession is only a map of where you went wrong. It is not the road back.*

The litter groaned against the packed earth, the wooden frame creaking in a rhythm that sounded suspiciously like a complaint. Isla had arranged the cushions with the same fastidious care she applied to her field-book, tucking a wool blanket under the elbow of the man who lay there, propped up by pillows and a terrible, quiet dignity. Master Orrin Vasht had not complained on the journey. He had merely adjusted his hat, which still sat at a precise angle despite the broken ankle, and watched the world pass by with the detached interest of a man observing a map being drawn.

When the litter reached the mill-house, the door opened before Mags could touch the handle. Old Perrin Ashdown stood there, his stick tapping a slow, irregular beat on the threshold. He did not look at the litter. He did not look at Isla. His small, white-whiskered face fixed entirely on the man in the chair, and the air in the doorway went still, the dust motes hanging motionless in the shaft of sunlight.

"Orrin Vasht," Perrin said. His voice was not loud, but it carried the gravity of a deep sounding. "You’ve gone grey."

Vasht’s hand, resting on the edge of the litter, tightened. His knuckles whitened. For a long moment, neither man moved. The light caught the fine hairs on their forearms, frozen in the sudden silence. Then Vasht spoke, his voice rough, stripped of its usual professional polish. "Yes, Perrin. I have."

Isla watched them, her chest tight with a sensation like a miscalculated angle. She had expected anger, or perhaps a cold, polite dismissal. She had not expected this: a recognition so profound it felt like a physical blow. She looked at the bundle of papers Vasht had clutched to his chest the entire time, the edges of the sheets frayed and stained with travel dirt. Whatever was in that bundle, she realized with a sudden, icy clarity, was not just a report. It was a confession.

"Master Vasht," Isla said, her voice sounding thinner than she intended. "We have tea. And Mags has made a pie. It is not as good as the Guild’s, but it is warm."

Vasht looked at her then. His grey eyes were sharp, intelligent, and terribly tired. "I would like to see the valley," he said quietly. "Before I see the pie."
pages.image: An old man in a battered felt hat and grey coat sits in a wooden litter, looking intently at a tiny, wiry elderly man with white whiskers standing in a doorway, while a teenage girl in a mustard coat watches from the side with worry.

pages.text:
The mill-house smelled of woodsmoke and damp stone. Isla had lit a fire in the small iron stove, and the flames cast long, dancing shadows against the rough-hewn beams. Vasht sat in the only chair that didn't creak, his ankle elevated on a stack of old ledgers. The bundle of papers lay on the table between them, untouched. Isla had poured tea. The cups sat cooling, a thin film of skin forming on the surface.

"I was nineteen," Vasht said. He did not look at the papers. He looked at the fire. "I was a junior clerk in the Office of Verification. My job was to check the field-books against the benchmarks. It was tedious work. I hated it. I wanted to be out in the field, measuring the world, not sitting in a room smelling of ink and dust."

He paused, stirring the tea without lifting the spoon. "The inspector’s report on Hester Corrin’s sheet was signed by three senior masters. They were formidable men. Men I feared. They told me that the closing error was undeniable. That the valley had drifted because the survey was flawed. They told me to sign. I asked for the benchmark data. They gave it to me. I checked it. And I found..." He stopped. His hand trembled slightly, a fine vibration that ran through his forearm.

"Found what?" Isla asked. Her voice was steady. Her hands, under the table, were not.

"That the benchmark in Vell had been reset two years prior," Vasht said. "A minor adjustment. A hair's breadth. But for a survey of that precision, a hair is a chasm. The valley hadn't drifted, Isla. The city had moved. Or rather, the point from which we measured the city had moved. And nobody had told the field parties. Nobody had told the apprentices. I was told to say nothing. I was told that if I spoke, my career was over. I was nineteen. I was afraid. And so I signed."

The silence that followed was heavy, suffocating. Isla felt the words settle in her stomach, cold and hard. She thought of Hester Corrin, a name she had carried like a stone in her pocket for two years, a name that had been synonymous with failure, with shame, with a mistake that had unmade a whole valley. And she realized, with a sudden, violent clarity, that the stone had been in her pocket all along.
pages.image: An old man in a grey coat sits in a chair by a fire, looking down at his trembling hands, while a teenage girl in a mustard coat sits across from him, her face pale and her eyes wide with shock, a cup of tea steaming between them.

pages.text:
"I trusted you," Isla said. The words tumbled out before she could check them, sharp and jagged as a poorly cut chain link. "You were the only person in the Guild who looked at my work and saw something worth keeping. I trusted you with my future, and with my name."

She stood up, and the chair scraped back against the stone floor with a harsh, grating sound that seemed to tear the air in two. Vasht did not flinch, nor did he look up. He simply sat there, a small, grey figure in the center of the room, and let the silence do its work.

"You let me carry it," Isla continued, her voice rising and cracking on the edges. "You let me believe that my family’s name was a stain. That I was the odd one out, the scholarship girl, the one who had to prove herself three times over. And you knew. You knew the whole time. You just watched me struggle, watched me try to fix a mistake that wasn't there."

She was breathing hard, her chest heaving against the tight buttons of her coat. The anger was a physical thing, hot and bright, burning in her throat like swallowed fire. She wanted to take the bundle of papers and tear them into shreds, to send them flying into the stove. But she didn't, because she knew, with a terrible, lucid precision, that it wouldn't matter. The damage was done. The years of doubt, the years of feeling less than, the years of apologizing for her own existence in a room full of boys who had never once been told they were inadequate, were all still there, waiting for her.

Vasht finally looked up. His eyes were wet, though he did not blink. "I chose you to take this journey," he said softly, "because I wanted someone honest to find it out. I wanted you to be the one to know the truth. I wanted you to have the strength to carry it. I was... cowardly. But I hoped you would be braver than I was."

Isla stared at him. The anger did not leave her; it settled deeper, into her bones, into the place where her shame used to live. She looked at the papers on the table, then at the fire, and finally at the door.

"Get out," she said. Her voice was quiet, the quietest, most dangerous thing she had ever said.
pages.image: A teenage girl in a mustard coat stands with her back to the viewer, facing an old man in a grey coat who sits slumped in a chair, his head bowed, in a dimly lit room with a fire burning in the stove.

pages.text:
The orchard stood thick with leaf under the grey sky, its blossom long since gone to small green fruit, while the ground below lay littered with fallen petals and the odd windfall. Isla walked among them, her boots crunching on the dry leaves, not knowing where she was going other than away from the room, the house, and the man who had known the truth and kept it.

She found a stump and sat, legs crossed, hands wrapped tightly around her knees, the cold air biting at her exposed neck. She did not cry, feeling too tired for the effort, and noticed only a hollow, empty space in her chest where her heart should have been.

Footsteps approached, and she did not look up, recognizing the gait, the slight limp, the way the boots scuffed the earth. Joss. He did not speak, nor did he ask what was wrong; he simply found a stump of his own, a few feet away, and sat down. He took a carpenter's pencil from behind one ear and began to whittle a small splinter from the wood, his movements slow and deliberate.

The silence stretched between them, comfortable and safe, the kind that exists only between people who do not need to fill the air with words. Isla watched the pencil shavings curl and fall to the ground, then watched Joss’s hands, steady and sure, and thought about the bridge he was building, the way he thought in loads and forces, in the things that held and the things that broke.

"He should have told me," she said finally, her voice rough, scraped raw.

Joss stopped whittling and looked at her, his sandy hair falling into his eyes. "Yes," he said. "And he's also the person who taught you to check things three times, which is how you caught him."

Isla looked at him, and a strange, twisted smile played on her lips. "Is that supposed to comfort me?"

"No," Joss said. "It's supposed to be true. And you hate it when I'm not true."

Isla laughed, a short, sharp sound, barely more than a breath, but it was something, and it was a beginning.
pages.image: A teenage girl in a mustard coat sits on a tree stump in an orchard, looking at a tall boy with sandy hair in a rust-red shirt who sits on another stump, holding a pencil, both of them looking down at the ground.

pages.text:
Isla returned to the mill-house before Joss. She did not apologize, nor did she ask for forgiveness. Walking in, she closed the door and stood in the center of the room, looking at Vasht. He remained in the chair, his hat slightly askew. Looking up, he did not appear afraid; he looked resigned.

"I am not ready to forgive you," Isla said. "I do not know if I will be. I do not know if forgiveness is something that can be given so easily, for a thing so large. But I am going to close this survey. I am going to prove that Hester Corrin was right. And I am going to do it with the same meticulous care that you taught me. And when that is done, when the truth is in the ink and the land is fixed, then we will talk about what this means for you. And for me."

Vasht nodded. It was a small, slow movement, but it carried the gravity of his relief. "That is a fair deal," he said.

"I need you to teach me," Isla said, moving to the table. She pushed the bundle of papers aside and pulled out her own field-book. "I need you to teach me the Guild’s inspection procedures. Every clause. Every loophole. I need to know how they will try to dispute the final sheet. I need to know how to trap them in their own honesty."

Vasht’s eyes widened slightly. He looked at her, and for a moment, the old man was gone, replaced by the master surveyor, sharp and precise. "That is a dangerous thing to learn," he said. "The Guild does not like to be trapped."

"Neither do I," Isla said. She picked up her pen. "But I have time. And I have a steady hand. And I have a truth that is bigger than any of them."

She began to write. The sound of the pen on paper was the only sound in the room, a steady, rhythmic scratch that sounded like a heartbeat. Vasht watched her, and he did not look tired. He looked alive.
